brief.topic: The Same Step Can Reach Different Heights

s01: A rotating ray crosses a straight guide.
From the crossing, take the same fixed step along the ray.
That moving endpoint draws a curve.
The step keeps its length while its direction changes.
It is measured along the ray, not straight upward from the guide.
The whole step now adds height.
Tilt it sixty degrees away from upright.
Only half the step now contributes to height.
Compare with a different rule: always take the step straight upward.
Those endpoints would sit on a straight line parallel to the guide.
Both rules use the same step length, but they measure in different directions.
Its trace is one branch of a conchoid.
As the direction changes, the height changes with it.
Even a simple instruction can contain a hidden choice of geometry.

creative.audience: Curious teens and adults; no specialist prerequisites.
creative.learning_goal: A fixed ray-wise offset from a line creates a conchoid branch; its perpendicular height gain is the step length times cosine of the angle from the normal.
creative.question: Does a fixed step beyond a line always produce a parallel line?

scenes.narration:
A rotating ray crosses a straight guide. From the crossing, take the same fixed step along the ray. That moving endpoint draws a curve.

The step keeps its length while its direction changes. It is measured along the ray, not straight upward from the guide. That small distinction matters.

Turn the ray upright. The whole step now adds height. Tilt it sixty degrees away from upright. Only half the step now contributes to height.

Compare with a different rule: always take the step straight upward. Those endpoints would sit on a straight line parallel to the guide. Both rules use the same step length, but they measure in different directions.

Return to the slanting step. Its trace is one branch of a conchoid. As the direction changes, the height changes with it. Even a simple instruction can contain a hidden choice of geometry.
